# It’s Just One Assignment, Except It Isn’t

Last night Jess texted me, “It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.”

Half the group chat more or less agreed with her. I started typing replies to everyone and then stopped, because I could feel myself turning one complicated thing into fifteen increasingly annoying text messages. So this is my attempt to explain it once, properly. It’s technically for everyone, but it’s mostly for Jess.

Also: I’m not mad at her. Just to get that out of the way.

For anyone who hasn’t heard the play-by-play, I teach two sections of U.S. History II, both juniors, at Cobb Street High. For the past four years, one of my assignments has been an oral history project about Boston busing and school desegregation in 1974–76. Students interview someone in their family or neighborhood who remembers that period, make a ten-minute recording, and write a two-page reflection.

That’s the whole project. It is not a trial. Nobody has to deliver a verdict on a relative. The reflection is about what they heard, what surprised them, how the person’s memory fits with what we’ve learned, and sometimes what the person didn’t want to talk about.

This year, a parent emailed my principal, Dr. Halvorsen, and cc’d a school committee member. She said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” Halvorsen would like me to quietly drop it.

I’m not going to.

I do have a meeting with Halvorsen and the parent on Thursday, November 19, at 3:15. I’m not walking in there to tell her she’s wrong and I’m right. Actually, I think she has a point about pressure.

If you come from a family where certain subjects are radioactive, being sent home by your teacher with a recording device is not neutral. Maybe Grandma doesn’t want to remember 1974. Maybe Mom is furious about something her father did, and her sixteen-year-old does not need to be dropped into the middle of it for a history grade. Maybe the person a student most wants to interview says no, and then the student has to explain that to me. I can say “no family drama required” until I’m blue in the face, but teenagers are good at hearing the expectations underneath my expectations.

So I’m changing the part that needs changing. Students can still do the original interview, but there will be an explicit alternate option: interview a librarian or archivist, or—if I can get the necessary permissions—work with recorded interviews from previous years. Nobody will have to interview a family member. Nobody will have to explain why they aren’t interviewing a family member. The alternate won’t be a lesser assignment or require a private confession to me about their home life.

But dropping the project altogether is a different thing.

The textbook gives Boston busing one paragraph. One paragraph, in the city where these kids live. You could read it and come away thinking there was a disagreement, some people were upset, and eventually everyone moved on. That is not what happened, and it is definitely not what people remember.

I want my students to hear what happens when history is not a paragraph. When somebody’s voice changes halfway through a sentence. When a person says “we were just trying to protect our neighborhood” and the student has to sit with everything those words contain. When somebody admits they were scared, or cruel, or young, or all three. When a story doesn’t resolve neatly just because the recorder is running.

In 2023, one of my students, D., interviewed his grandmother. She had driven a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family. Not her kids, not her husband, nobody. D. played forty seconds of the recording for the class, and afterward nobody said anything for what felt like a full minute.

I know teachers are always saying that. “You could have heard a pin drop.” Usually somebody’s pencil rolls off a desk and ruins it. This was different. They were still trying to understand that this ordinary woman they had heard on a recording had been inside this thing they thought belonged to photographs in textbooks.

Letting Boston’s history disappear into family silence is not the same thing as healing it.

Last year, a girl found out that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus.

Finding out that someone in your family did something ugly is not automatically a beautiful learning experience. Sometimes it’s just upsetting. I want to be clear that I don’t look at a shaken sixteen-year-old and think, *Excellent, the primary sources are working.*

She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection ended up being the best thing I read all year, not because she wrote “my uncle was bad” or found some tidy way to forgive him, but because she refused to make it simple. She wrote about loving someone whose story she now had to understand differently. She noticed what he left out. She asked who got to call themselves a good person afterward.

Do I think the students who are most uncomfortable with this history are often the ones who most need a way to think about it honestly? Yes. I do.

But that does not mean discomfort is proof I’m doing something right. And I don’t get to force anyone to have a conversation with their family because I think it would be good for them. I don’t get to decide that a grandparent owes my class a memory. That’s the line. Offering an alternative can’t be a loophole I add resentfully while hoping nobody takes it. It has to be real.

Jess knows I’m not naturally good at being the brave teacher in a movie. We met when we were student teaching at the same school in 2012. She saw me spend twenty minutes looking for a stack of quizzes that I was holding. She left teaching in 2019 and now does HR at a biotech in Cambridge, which means she also has a much more realistic understanding than I do of what administrators mean when they start using phrases like “finding a path forward.”

And she isn’t wrong that I could get burned.

Yes, I’ve been tenured since 2021. No, that does not make me invincible. Halvorsen still controls my schedule. Halvorsen still has a say in who gets AP. There are roughly a thousand ways to make a teacher’s life smaller without technically firing them, and I am aware of every single one of them at three in the morning.

I’m scared a little. Not in an inspiring way. I keep composing sentences for Thursday while brushing my teeth and then thinking, *Well, that would sound insane out loud.* I would very much like everyone to be reasonable and for this to cost me nothing.

But if I quietly remove the project now, what exactly am I teaching? That this part of Boston’s history is fine to cover as long as nobody remembers it personally? That one paragraph is safer? That the purpose of learning history is to make sure nobody goes home with an uncomfortable question?

I don’t think that.

I also don’t think the parent is villainous for wanting to protect her kid. I want her to leave the meeting knowing I heard the word “pressure” and took it seriously. I’m hoping she can hear me when I say the answer is to loosen the assignment, not erase the history.

Jess, I’m not asking you to agree that this is the hill I should die on. I’d especially appreciate nobody using the phrase “die on a hill” around my actual job.

I just want you to understand why “it’s one assignment” doesn’t quite work for me. It is one assignment, yes. It’s also four years of students learning that history is something people carry, sometimes badly, sometimes silently, sometimes for fifty years before their grandson asks the right question. I can make it easier to say no without making the whole thing disappear.

I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting.
